# AI Receptionist for a Dental Practice: What to Look for Before You Buy
Source: https://clinekthealth.com/blog/ai-receptionist-for-dental-practice
Published: 2026-08-14

Direct answer: An AI receptionist for a dental practice is software that answers every inbound call, texts back missed calls, and books directly into your practice management system, so a caller reaches a live response even when your front desk is on another line, at lunch, or closed for the day. For a dental office, that means new-patient inquiries, hygiene recall calls, and after-hours emergencies all get a first response instead of a ring that goes nowhere.

Key takeaways: Dental call volume is heavier and more schedule-sensitive than most medical practices, because hygiene recall, new-patient intake, and same-day emergency calls all compete for the same phone line. The best evaluation criterion is not whether it can talk, it is whether it books correctly into your specific practice management system without a staff member re-entering the appointment. Front-desk staffing gaps make this a coverage decision as much as a technology one; many practices run with a single trained front-desk employee and zero backup when that person is out. Multi-location dental groups and DSOs need to evaluate consistency across locations, not just performance at one site. Clinical judgment calls, active pain, allergic reactions, post-surgical complications, and insurance disputes still belong with a trained human, and any AI receptionist worth buying should say so, not try to handle everything.

Section summaries: Three numbers explain the buying urgency: only 68% of new-patient calls to a dental practice get answered, and of those only 42% turn into a booked appointment (Peerlogic); roughly 9 in 10 dental practices report that hiring front-desk and clinical support staff is still hard, per ADA Health Policy Institute data cited in the ADA's 2026 economic reporting; and DSO-affiliated practices are projected to grow from 23% of the U.S. dental market in 2022 to roughly 39% by 2026 (L.E.K. Consulting). At minimum, an AI receptionist answers or responds to every inbound call and text, understands intent (new patient, existing patient, emergency, insurance question, reschedule), and either books directly or routes to a human with context captured; for dental specifically that includes recognizing hygiene recall callbacks and distinguishing a routine cleaning request from a same-day pain call. Dental deployments differ from medical ones in call rhythm (routine schedulable calls plus a smaller urgent pain/trauma stream) and in integration (a smaller, more standardized set of practice management systems: Dentrix, Eaglesoft, Open Dental, Curve, Denticon). A six-step evaluation: call it after hours and on a busy morning; test a same-day pain call; confirm it writes directly into your PMS; check hygiene recall handling; ask what it does not handle; and test consistency across locations if you run more than one. What should still go to a human: active pain, allergic reactions, post-surgical complications, billing disputes, insurance appeals, and any upset patient. Proof: Baldwin Bone and Joint, a cross-specialty orthopedic proof point (no dental-specific quantitative result exists in canon), generated 263 qualified surgical leads and 159 booked appointments in a single quarter, a 60% booking rate, using Clinekt's Inbound, Recall, and Outbound agents together.

FAQ digest: An AI receptionist does not replace a dental front-desk team; it handles calls and texts the team cannot get to and hands off anything requiring judgment or a personal touch. Whether it works with a specific practice management system depends on the vendor; always demo against the actual PMS and confirm the appointment writes back without manual re-entry. Any vendor handling patient calls and scheduling data should speak clearly to HIPAA compliance, including a signed Business Associate Agreement. Unlike a legacy answering service, which takes a message for a callback, an AI receptionist books directly into the schedule during the same call. Multi-location practices and DSOs should specifically ask about consistency across sites: shared reporting, per-location configuration, and steady quality, which matters more every year as DSO affiliation grows.

# AI Voice Agent for a Dental Practice: What to Look for Before You Buy
Source: https://clinekthealth.com/blog/ai-voice-agent-for-dental-practice
Published: 2026-08-17

Direct answer: An AI voice agent for a dental practice is only worth buying if it can hold a real dental call, not the routine cleaning-booking demo every vendor shows, and prove that more of those calls turn into kept appointments once it starts answering. A demo caller who wants a six-month cleaning proves almost nothing; the call that decides the contract is a patient in pain, a recall callback, or a question the front desk would normally answer by looking at the chart.

Key takeaways: Test the agent on a pain call and a recall callback, not a routine booking request, since those two call types expose more than any scripted demo will. Roughly a third of new-patient calls into a dental practice go unanswered, and less than half of the ones that do connect turn into a booked visit (Peerlogic, 2026). Close to 3 in 10 calls into a practice already arrive outside business hours (NextPhone, 2026), and a pain call at 9pm needs more than a message taken for the morning. Medical and dental assistants remain the hardest role to recruit according to nearly half of practice leaders (MGMA, 2025), which is a large part of why dental phones go unanswered in the first place. DSO-affiliated practices are projected to grow from 23% of the U.S. dental market to roughly 39% by 2026 (L.E.K. Consulting), so more dental buyers are evaluating a voice agent for ten locations at once, not one.

Section summaries: A six-point evaluation checklist: run a real dental call describing pain, a broken filling, or swelling instead of a cleaning-booking script; test a hygiene recall callback and confirm the agent recognizes the returning-patient context; confirm live write-back into the practice's actual PMS (Dentrix, Eaglesoft, Open Dental, Curve, Denticon); check the after-hours pain-call behavior specifically, a same-day slot offer versus a next-morning message; require a business associate agreement scoped to the voice channel by name; and test consistency across sites for any multi-location or DSO buyer. A dental voice agent needs logic a generic one misses: recall calls are not new-patient calls, pain calls need triage logic rather than default booking logic, insurance questions need a clear escalation boundary, and multi-location consistency matters more here given DSO growth. Why the phone goes unanswered: the same staffing math that makes medical assistants the hardest role to recruit (MGMA, 2025) hits dental front desks, which often run with one trained employee and no backup, and the call-outcome data confirms it: only 68% of new-patient dental calls get answered and only 42% of those convert to a booking (Peerlogic, 2026), while 28.5% of calls arrive outside business hours (NextPhone, 2026) against Clinekt's own 82% after-hours booking-attempt figure. Proof: Baldwin Bone and Joint, a cross-specialty orthopedic proof point (no dental-specific quantitative result exists in canon), turned 263 qualified surgical leads into 159 booked appointments in a single quarter, a 60% booking rate, using Clinekt's Inbound and Recall agents.

FAQ digest: An AI voice agent for a dental practice answers the phone, recognizes intent (new patient, recall callback, pain call), and books, reschedules, or cancels directly in the PMS rather than only taking a message. It is the voice-specific slice of a broader AI receptionist deployment, which also covers text and web chat and practice management system integration more broadly. Patients generally accept an AI agent on a pain call when it identifies itself immediately, recognizes urgency, and hands off fast rather than pretending to offer clinical advice. A voice agent does not replace the front-desk team; it absorbs recall callbacks, routine booking, and basic insurance questions so staff handle judgment calls. Multi-location dental groups and DSOs should test consistency, not just capability, across every location on the same phone number pattern.

# AI Software for Orthopedic Practices: What to Look for Before You Buy
Source: https://clinekthealth.com/blog/ai-software-for-orthopedic-practices
Published: 2026-08-18

Direct answer: AI software for an orthopedic practice means four functions working as one system: a front desk that answers and routes every call, scheduling logic that understands subspecialty and visit type, referral capture that turns a fax or portal message into a booked appointment, and reactivation that works the list of patients who never called back. Buying any one function alone solves a quarter of the problem; buying all four as separate, disconnected tools trades one integration headache for four.

Key takeaways: "AI software for orthopedic practices" spans four functions (front desk/phone coverage, scheduling, referral management, patient reactivation), not a single tool. Front-office and medical-assistant turnover, not call volume alone, is the operational driver pushing practices to evaluate this as one category. Roughly two out of three specialty referrals never become a completed visit when nobody owns the follow-up loop, the single largest orthopedic-specific stake in the category. Test subspecialty and visit-type routing specifically, since scheduling logic built for a general primary-care calendar breaks on an orthopedic one. Practices seeing real results run these four functions against the same patient list as one connected system, not as four separate subscriptions.

Section summaries: Four distinct functions get sold under the "orthopedic AI software" umbrella: an AI front desk / orthopedic patient engagement software that answers and routes calls; AI scheduling that books the right visit type by subspecialty, imaging status, referral requirements, and payer authorization; referral management that tracks a referral from arrival to completed visit; and patient reactivation that works the list of patients who have not returned. Three data points explain the current timing: a May 2025 MGMA Stat poll of 357 practice leaders found 29% reported increased turnover, concentrated in reception and medical-assistant roles; a December 2025 MGMA Stat poll of 236 practice leaders found phone access named a top-tier 2026 patient-access priority (22%) alongside no-shows, online scheduling, and wait times; and a study of 103,737 referral scheduling attempts at a large academic health system found only 34.8% resulted in a completed appointment (Patel et al., Journal of General Internal Medicine, 2018). Separately, front-office turnover hit 40% across medical practices in 2022, the highest of any staff category (MGMA, 2023), and 82% of patients try to book care outside a practice's regular office hours. A six-point evaluation checklist: ask which of the four functions a vendor's tool actually covers; test subspecialty and visit-type routing on a real scenario; ask how a referral is tracked from arrival to completed visit; confirm after-hours escalation behavior for anything describing symptoms; check EHR/scheduling-system write-back, not just read access; and ask for a completion number, not an activity number. Most of the category is still sold as point solutions with gaps between tools; Clinekt's Inbound, Recall, and Outbound agents work the same patient record from three directions (inbound calls/referrals, dormant-patient reactivation, and net-new demand) so nothing sits in a gap. Proof: Baldwin Bone and Joint, an orthopedic practice running Clinekt's full patient activation system, generated 263 qualified surgical leads and booked 159 appointments in a single recent quarter, a 60% booking rate, driven by full coverage across calls, referrals, and scheduling rather than any one function in isolation.

FAQ digest: Orthopedic AI software is a category of tools automating front-desk phone coverage, scheduling, referral management, or patient reactivation, individually or as a connected system, with no single standard definition yet. An AI front desk is one function inside the broader category, covering phone/message intake, and does not by itself guarantee scheduling logic, referral tracking, or reactivation. Orthopedic AI software does not replace front-desk staff; it absorbs high-volume repeatable work so staff handle complaints, complex authorizations, and clinical conversations. Orthopedic scheduling differs from general medical scheduling because it has to account for subspecialty, visit type, imaging status, referral requirements, and payer authorization at once. Evaluation and deployment should run as a real pilot against a practice's own call and referral volume over a couple of weeks, with deployment itself measured in days once a vendor is chosen.

# Orthopedic Patient Reactivation Software: What to Look for Before You Buy
Source: https://clinekthealth.com/blog/orthopedic-patient-reactivation-software
Published: 2026-08-19

Direct answer: Orthopedic patient reactivation software has to do more than send a reminder text. It has to find the post-op patients, imaging holds, and surgical consults sitting quiet in an EHR, reach them in a way that gets a real reply, and carry that reply through to a booked visit. Generic recall tools built for annual cleanings or wellness visits treat every dormant patient the same way, and an orthopedic list is not that simple.

Key takeaways: Orthopedic reactivation software needs to segment by clinical urgency, not just days since last visit, since a missed post-op follow-up is a different priority than a lapsed imaging order. Missed pre-operative and post-operative appointments carry a measurable clinical risk in orthopedics, not just a scheduling inconvenience. Text-first outreach with a real conversation behind it reaches dormant patients faster than a one-way reminder, because most of them have a question before they will rebook. The best reactivation tools finish the job: they carry the reply through screening and into a booked slot instead of handing a "yes" back to a queue. Reactivation is one of three places orthopedic practices lose patients, alongside missed inbound calls and unworked referrals, so software that only reactivates fixes one leak of three.

Section summaries: A retrospective cohort study of 6,776 primary total knee arthroplasty patients found that patients with three or more no-show appointments before surgery had 1.5 times higher odds of a surgical site infection than patients who always attended, a statistically significant finding (Journal of Arthroplasty, June 2023); pre-op and post-op attendance is part of the surgical outcome, not administrative housekeeping. Staffing makes the problem harder to solve by hand: a May 2025 MGMA Stat poll of 357 practice leaders found 29% reported turnover had increased year over year, with reception and medical-assistant roles named first among those seeing higher turnover (MGMA, May 2025), and 82% of patients try to book care outside a practice's regular office hours. Four things separate purpose-built orthopedic reactivation from a generic recall campaign tool: clinical-urgency segmentation, subspecialty and visit-type awareness, a conversation rather than a one-way message, and a path straight to a booked slot instead of a queued task. A six-point evaluation checklist: pull the practice's own dormant list first, separating the clinical-risk segment (missed post-op/pre-op) from routine dormant patients; ask how the tool segments by clinical urgency; test a real post-op scenario with a mid-conversation clinical question; confirm the tool books the appointment itself rather than routing a "yes" back to staff; check EHR write-back for the practice's specific system; and ask for a completion number tied to a quarter, not an activity number. Reactivation alone does not solve orthopedic patient leakage: dormant patients are one of three leak points alongside missed inbound calls and unworked referrals, which is why Clinekt built Recall as one of three connected agents (Inbound, Recall, Outbound) working the same patient record rather than as a standalone reactivation product. Proof: Baldwin Bone and Joint, an orthopedic practice running Clinekt's full patient activation system, generated 263 qualified surgical leads and booked 159 appointments in a single recent quarter, a 60% booking rate, with reactivation as one input alongside inbound call handling and referral follow-through.

FAQ digest: Orthopedic patient reactivation software identifies patients in an orthopedic EHR who have gone dormant, including lapsed post-op follow-ups, stalled imaging orders, and consults that never converted to a scheduled procedure, and reaches out to bring them back onto the schedule. It differs from general patient recall because orthopedic reactivation has to account for surgical timelines and clinical urgency, where a missed pre-op or post-op appointment carries a measurable outcome risk. It replaces the repetitive, high-volume part of identifying the list and sending the first outreach; a tool that also carries the conversation and books the visit removes most of the manual follow-up work, while anything requiring clinical judgment should still escalate to staff. Text-first outreach consistently gets a faster reply for time-sensitive orthopedic follow-ups than email alone, though the right tool should support both. Most of the list can be segmented and a first outreach wave sent within days of go-live, with the clinically urgent segment prioritized first.

# Orthopedic Patient Engagement Software: What to Look for Before You Buy
Source: https://clinekthealth.com/blog/orthopedic-patient-engagement-software
Published: 2026-08-20

Direct answer: Orthopedic patient engagement software has to do more than send appointment reminders and satisfaction surveys. It has to carry a patient through scheduling, pre-op and post-op check-ins, referral follow-through, and reactivation, all inside one connected record. Generic patient engagement platforms built for primary care treat every touchpoint the same way, and an orthopedic patient's journey is not that simple.

Key takeaways: Orthopedic patient engagement software needs to span scheduling, pre/post-op check-ins, referral intake, and reactivation, not just messaging and reminders. Peer-reviewed orthopedic research links structured perioperative engagement platforms to measurably better outcomes, not just higher satisfaction scores. Generic healthcare engagement platforms are not built for surgical timelines, and it shows in how they segment and prioritize patients. The best orthopedic engagement tools finish the job: a patient reply leads to a booked or rescheduled visit inside the same conversation, not a queued task. Engagement software is one of three places orthopedic practices lose patients, alongside missed inbound calls and unworked referrals, so a tool that only engages fixes one leak of three.

Section summaries: A multicenter observational study of an orthopedic mHealth engagement platform across 10 practice sites found patients enrolled in structured perioperative engagement had a 45.4% relative reduction in 90-day hospital readmissions and a 54.4% relative reduction in 90-day complications compared with non-enrolled patients (Rosner et al., Journal of Arthroplasty, 2018). A separate randomized study of an automated SMS-based check-in tool for total joint patients found the engaged group exercised more consistently, reported better pain scores, discontinued narcotic pain medication earlier, and called the clinic less often than the control group (Campbell et al., Journal of Bone and Joint Surgery American, 2019). Four things separate a purpose-built orthopedic engagement system from a general platform: perioperative-aware messaging that triggers off the surgical date, two-way conversation rather than one-way broadcast, referral and reactivation built in rather than bolted on, and a path to a booked or rescheduled visit rather than a queued task. A six-point evaluation checklist: map the practice's own patient journey and mark which touchpoints are manual; ask how the tool handles a real clinical question; test referral intake specifically for after-hours arrivals; confirm the tool books or reschedules the visit itself; check EHR write-back for the practice's specific system; and ask for outcome numbers tied to a quarter, not just messages sent. Proof: Baldwin Bone and Joint, an orthopedic practice running Clinekt's full patient activation system, generated 263 qualified surgical leads and booked 159 appointments in a single recent quarter, a 60% booking rate, reflecting inbound call handling, referral follow-through, and reactivation working together rather than a messaging platform operating alone.

FAQ digest: Orthopedic patient engagement software manages patient communication and scheduling actions across the full orthopedic journey, from first inbound call through referral intake, pre-op and post-op check-ins, and reactivation of dormant patients, inside one connected record. It differs from a general patient engagement platform because orthopedic engagement has to trigger off a surgical timeline, handle referral intake, and support a two-way conversation, since perioperative patients ask real clinical questions a one-way reminder cannot answer. It replaces the repetitive, high-volume part of outreach and initial triage; a tool that also carries the conversation to a booked visit removes most of the manual follow-up, while anything requiring clinical judgment should still escalate to staff. Published orthopedic research has linked structured perioperative engagement platforms to fewer 90-day readmissions and complications, along with better reported pain control and fewer clinic calls in a randomized study of automated post-op check-ins. Inbound call handling and referral intake typically start working from go-live, while perioperative check-in sequences and dormant-patient reactivation take a bit longer depending on surgical schedule and dormant list size.

# Orthopedic Referral Management Software: What to Look for Before You Buy
Source: https://clinekthealth.com/blog/orthopedic-referral-management-software
Published: 2026-08-21

Direct answer: Orthopedic referral management software has to do more than digitize a fax queue. It has to route each referral to the right subspecialty, work imaging and prior-authorization holds, and get the patient onto a surgeon's schedule before they call a competitor. A generic referral tool built for primary care treats every incoming referral as one queue worked in order, and orthopedics is not that simple.

Key takeaways: Orthopedic referral management software needs subspecialty-aware routing across spine, sports medicine, joint replacement, and hand or foot and ankle, not one shared intake queue. Peer-reviewed research shows surgical conversion rate varies enormously by referral source, which most referral tools ignore when they route every referral the same way. Imaging and prior-authorization holds are where orthopedic referrals stall longest, and generic referral software rarely automates that step. The best orthopedic referral tools close the loop: a referral becomes a booked consult inside the same workflow, not a fax that sits in a queue until someone works it. Referral management fixes one of three places orthopedic practices lose patients, alongside missed inbound calls and patients who never get reactivated.

Section summaries: A systematic review and meta-analysis of 28 studies covering 5,358 patients found surgical conversion rate varies sharply by referral source: 23% across all doctor referrals combined, 28% from general practitioners, 61% from physiotherapy-led screening services, and 70% from sports physicians (Health Services Insights, 2024). A study of emergency-department referrals into orthopedic surgery found that even after implementing a three-tier urgency system, only 45.1% of referrals completed scheduling, up from 41.5% before the system existed, across 856 total referrals (Western Journal of Emergency Medicine, 2025). Four things separate a purpose-built orthopedic referral system from a generic inbox: subspecialty-aware intake, imaging and prior-authorization workflow, referral-source-aware prioritization, and a path to a booked consult with EHR write-back. A six-point evaluation checklist: test subspecialty routing with a real referral; ask how imaging and prior-authorization holds are tracked; confirm referral source is captured and used; check callback speed for after-hours referrals; confirm EHR write-back for the booked visit; and ask for a conversion number, not a volume number. Referral management alone does not fix orthopedic patient leakage: practices lose patients in three places (missed inbound calls, unworked referrals, and dormant patients who never get reactivated), which is why Clinekt built referral handling as part of three connected agents (Inbound, Recall, Outbound) working the same patient record rather than as a standalone inbox. Proof: Baldwin Bone and Joint, an orthopedic practice running Clinekt's full patient activation system, generated 263 qualified surgical leads and booked 159 appointments in a single recent quarter, a 60% booking rate, reflecting referral follow-through, inbound call handling, and reactivation working together rather than a referral inbox operating alone.

FAQ digest: Orthopedic referral management software routes incoming orthopedic referrals to the right subspecialty, tracks imaging and prior-authorization holds, and carries the referral through to a scheduled and kept visit, instead of just logging that a referral arrived. It differs from general referral management software because orthopedic referrals need subspecialty routing across spine, sports medicine, joint replacement, and hand or foot and ankle, plus imaging and prior-authorization tracking a generic tool rarely automates. Referral source matters: published research found surgical conversion rate ranged from 23% for combined doctor referrals to 70% for sports-physician referrals. Many orthopedic referrals never get scheduled because they stall on imaging holds, prior authorization, and manual follow-up that never happens, not because patients decline care; one study found only 41.5% to 45.1% of ED-to-orthopedics referrals completed scheduling even with a formal urgency tier. It replaces the repetitive part of intake, routing, and status tracking; a tool that also carries the referral to a booked visit removes most of the manual chasing, while anything requiring clinical judgment should still escalate to staff.

# Orthopedic AI Scheduling Software: What to Look for Before You Buy
Source: https://clinekthealth.com/blog/orthopedic-ai-scheduling-software
Published: 2026-08-24

Direct answer: Orthopedic AI scheduling software is only worth buying if it knows the difference between a 15-minute follow-up and a 90-minute total joint consult, routes a shoulder complaint away from a spine surgeon's calendar automatically, and writes every booking directly into the EHR and OR schedule without a staff member re-entering it by hand. Generic medical scheduling tools can fill a calendar; very few hold the subspecialty logic and surgical block rules an orthopedic practice runs on.

Key takeaways: Test whether the software writes bookings, surgical block time, and cancellations directly into the practice management system and OR schedule, or just hands staff a request to enter by hand. Orthopedic scheduling needs subspecialty complaint-to-provider routing built in, so a shoulder complaint never lands on a spine surgeon's calendar. Case-duration and surgical block logic matter more here than in general medical scheduling, where most appointments are interchangeable. Cancellation-risk prediction works in orthopedic surgery, but the risk factors are specialty-specific and a generic model misses most of them. Ask for completion-rate reporting from an existing orthopedic customer, not booking-volume reporting from a generalist one.

Section summaries: A 2020 study in Arthroscopy, Sports Medicine, and Rehabilitation followed 571 patients scheduled for elective orthopedic sports medicine surgery and found 13.4% canceled and did not reschedule; the strongest predictors were age 46.5 or older, current smoking status, non-English-speaking status, no prior surgical history requiring anesthesia, and Medicare or Medicaid coverage, putting a modeled low-risk patient at 3.7% cancellation risk and a high-risk patient at 52.7%. A 2025 study in BMC Medical Informatics and Decision Making trained a machine learning model on 3,704 hip and knee arthroplasty cases and reached a mean absolute error of about 12 to 14 minutes per case, roughly a 22 to 23% average deviation from actual surgery time, tight enough to tighten block scheduling but not tight enough to book back-to-back cases on faith. A December 2025 MGMA Stat poll of 236 practice leaders found patient-access priorities split across no-shows (27%), online scheduling (24%), phone access (22%), and wait times (21%), with no single issue dominating; orthopedic practices carry all four at once. Four capabilities separate purpose-built orthopedic scheduling from a relabeled general tool: subspecialty routing, surgical block and case-duration logic, prerequisite handling (imaging, medical clearance, insurance authorization), and referral/post-op follow-through. A six-point evaluation checklist: watch a live write-back for a total joint consult and a same-day injection; review the subspecialty routing script; test surgical block scheduling specifically; ask what happens when the integration drops mid-conversation; require completion-rate reporting from an orthopedic customer; and run a real 60-to-90-day pilot. Proof: Baldwin Bone and Joint, a multi-provider orthopedic group using Clinekt's Inbound and Recall agents, turned 263 qualified surgical leads into 159 booked appointments, a 60% booking rate, in a single quarter, without adding front-desk headcount.

FAQ digest: Orthopedic AI scheduling software holds a conversation with a patient by phone, text, or web, screens for the right subspecialty and visit type, checks live availability against the EHR or practice management system, and writes the booking, reschedule, or cancellation back into that system directly, including surgical block and prerequisite logic a general scheduling tool does not carry. It needs to differ from general medical scheduling software because an orthopedic schedule runs several visit types with different lengths, rooms, and prerequisites at once, plus subspecialty routing across multiple surgeons under one roof. AI can predict orthopedic surgical cancellation risk with real accuracy: a 2020 study found risk ranging from 3.7% to 52.7% depending on a small set of demographic and clinical factors a general no-show model does not score. AI surgery-duration prediction is close but not exact: a 2025 arthroplasty study found predictions landed within about 12 to 14 minutes of actual surgery time on average. Evaluating a vendor means proving write-back on a sandbox of the practice's actual system, reviewing subspecialty routing logic line by line, testing surgical block scheduling specifically, and requiring completion-rate reporting from an existing orthopedic or surgical customer.

# Orthopedic Patient Leakage: Where It Happens and How to Stop It
Source: https://clinekthealth.com/blog/orthopedic-patient-leakage
Published: 2026-08-25

Direct answer: Orthopedic patient leakage is any patient who should have ended up on the schedule but did not, because a call went unanswered, a referral was routed to the wrong subspecialist before anyone looked at it, or a post-op patient who needed a follow-up simply stopped responding. It is three separate failure points that show up as one number: fewer patients on the calendar than referral volume and call volume should produce.

Key takeaways: Orthopedic leakage happens at three points: the call that never gets answered, the referral that never gets routed to the right subspecialist, and the post-op or dormant patient who goes quiet. No-show risk in orthopedic care is measurable and uneven across subspecialties, not random noise in the schedule. A meaningful share of orthopedic referrals are misdirected before a visit is ever booked, which counts as leakage even though the patient technically reached a clinic. Closing leakage is a workflow fix, not a marketing fix: same-day contact, subspecialty-correct routing, and a standing recall cadence close most of it. Track completion rate by referral source, not raw call or lead volume, as the number that proves leakage is actually closing.

Section summaries: A study of every scheduled appointment across calendar year 2016 at a single orthopedic multispecialty institution found an overall no-show rate of 11.5%, with statistically significant differences by patient age, race, and orthopedic subspecialty, but no significant difference by appointment time of day or month (Journal of Healthcare Management, 2018). A four-year retrospective analysis of 23,435 orthopedic outpatient referrals found that 29.6% of cases did not require primary orthopedic consultation at all, and an additional 58.2% were classified as cases that may or may not have needed to be seen primarily in an orthopedic clinic, leaving only 12.2% as clear must-see orthopedic cases (Cureus, 2019); routing errors lose capacity before a visit happens, and once a visit is booked correctly, subspecialty-specific no-show risk still needs managing on its own terms. Leakage concentrates in three places in an orthopedic practice: the front desk during and after business hours (roughly 82% of patients try to book outside office hours), the point where a referral gets matched to a subspecialist (a multi-provider group typically runs spine, joint replacement, sports medicine, and hand under one roof), and the months after surgery or a missed follow-up when a patient quietly falls off the schedule. Six fixes close most of it: answer every call the same day; route by subspecialty before offering a slot; confirm imaging, medical clearance, and insurance authorization before the visit lands on the calendar; run a standing recall cadence rather than a one-time reminder; track completion rate by referral source rather than raw volume; and pilot 60 to 90 days against real volume before committing long-term. Proof: Baldwin Bone and Joint, a multi-provider orthopedic group using Clinekt's Inbound and Recall agents, turned 263 qualified surgical leads into 159 booked appointments, a 60% booking rate, in a single quarter, without adding front-desk headcount.

---

# AI Receptionist for an Orthopedic Practice: What to Look for Before You Buy
Source: https://clinekthealth.com/blog/ai-receptionist-for-orthopedic-practice
Published: 2026-08-26

Direct answer: A good AI receptionist for an orthopedic practice answers nearly every inbound call, tells a routine post-op question apart from a surgical emergency, and routes each caller to the right subspecialty, coordinator, or escalation, without making the patient repeat themselves to a human afterward. That routing requirement is what separates an orthopedic-ready tool from a generic medical-office receptionist.

Key takeaways: Subspecialty-aware routing, not a single shared queue, is what separates an orthopedic-ready AI receptionist from a generic one. Front-office and medical-assistant turnover concentrates at the phone line, making full call coverage a staffing-resilience question as much as a patient-experience one. Phone access sits among practice leaders' top four patient-access priorities for 2026, alongside no-shows, online scheduling, and wait times. A meaningful share of calls that reach a surgeon directly are for questions a front desk could resolve, which is exactly what good triage logic should catch. Structured, consistent post-op communication measurably reduces how often patients call back at all.

Section summaries: In a May 2025 MGMA Stat poll of 357 practice leaders, 29% reported turnover had increased year over year, and among those seeing higher turnover, nearly all pointed first to their MA and reception teams. A December 2025 MGMA Stat poll of 236 practice leaders found patient access priorities split across no-shows (27%), online scheduling (24%), phone access (22%), and wait times (21%). A 2020 Cureus study of 207 orthopedic surgery patients found that among calls patients placed directly to their surgeon's cell phone, 45.2% were for non-urgent matters such as return-to-work questions and imaging scheduling, not surgical emergencies, exactly the volume good triage logic should intercept before it reaches a physician. A 2024 randomized controlled trial in Acta Orthopaedica followed 70 surgically treated orthopedic patients and found that consistent, team-based digital follow-up reduced patient-initiated phone calls from a mean of 2.3 per patient to 0.5, roughly a 78% drop, without hurting satisfaction, proving that structure around routine follow-up removes calls from the queue rather than just answering them faster. A six-point evaluation checklist: ask for subspecialty routing logic, not a single intake script; test post-op call handling specifically (routine wound-care question vs. red-flag symptom); confirm referral-call handling is separated from patient scheduling; check workers' compensation and insurance-authorization call handling; review escalation logic for ambiguous or emergency calls; and ask what data trains the model and where it is stored. Proof: Baldwin Bone and Joint, an orthopedic practice running Clinekt's full patient activation system, generated 263 qualified surgical leads and booked 159 appointments in a single recent quarter, a 60% booking rate.

FAQ digest: An AI receptionist for an orthopedic practice differs from a generalist one because subspecialty triage, post-op call handling, workers' comp documentation, and referral-call separation are orthopedic-specific requirements a generalist tool is not built to handle. It should distinguish a routine post-op question from a surgical emergency, tested directly in any vendor demo. It should route calls from referring physicians separately from patient scheduling calls. Whether it reduces calls that currently reach surgeons directly depends on triage quality, since research shows a meaningful share of direct-to-surgeon calls are for non-urgent matters a front desk could resolve. Deployment timelines depend on EHR/scheduling integration depth and how many subspecialty routing rules need configuring.

FAQ digest: Orthopedic patient leakage is the gap between the referrals, calls, and recall-eligible patients an orthopedic practice generates and the number who actually end up booked and seen, concentrated at unanswered calls, misrouted referrals, and dormant post-op patients. A four-year, 23,435-referral study found roughly 88% of referrals into orthopedic clinics were either unnecessary or ambiguous as primary orthopedic cases, meaning a large share of scheduled capacity was consumed by misrouted rather than correctly routed patients. No-show rates do differ by orthopedic subspecialty: a 2018 study found an overall 11.5% rate with significant differences by subspecialty, age, and race, but not by time of day or month. Referral leakage is the specific case of a referral that never converts into a completed visit; patient leakage is the broader category, covering referral leakage plus missed calls and dormant patients who never get recalled. Measuring improvement means tracking completion rate by referral source and subspecialty, not raw call or lead volume.

# AI Voice Agent for an Orthopedic Practice: What to Look for Before You Buy
Source: https://clinekthealth.com/blog/ai-voice-agent-for-orthopedic-practice
Published: 2026-08-27

Direct answer: An AI voice agent for an orthopedic practice is only worth buying if it can hold a real orthopedic call, not the routine new-patient booking demo every vendor shows, and prove that more of those calls turn into kept appointments once it starts answering. The call that decides the contract is the one where a patient three days post-op asks whether swelling is normal, a caller doesn't know whether pain is a hip or low-back problem, or the on-call line rings at midnight.

Key takeaways: Test the agent on a call that doesn't announce itself cleanly, an ambiguous injury call or a post-op question, not a scripted new-patient booking demo. Call volume itself is a clinical signal: each additional postoperative phone call was associated with roughly 19% higher odds of an ED visit after joint replacement surgery, in a study of nearly 11,000 patients (Ozdag et al., Arthroplasty Today, 2024). On-call orthopedic staff field an average of 8.6 patient calls per shift, most about pain, prescriptions, and wound concerns, and only about 1 in 25 of those calls results in an ED visit (Tideman et al., Annals of Medicine and Surgery, 2023). Close to 3 in 10 calls into a practice already arrive outside business hours (NextPhone, 2026). Medical assistants remain the toughest staff role to recruit, according to nearly half of practice leaders (MGMA, 2025).

Section summaries: A six-point evaluation checklist: run a real orthopedic call (ambiguous body-part pain, a post-op swelling question) instead of a new-patient booking script; test the escalation path on a call that sounds urgent (red-flag language should route to a human immediately); check whether the agent can see and book against provider-specific same-day/next-day surgical holds rather than only the general open calendar; confirm referral and imaging prerequisites are enforced before booking; require a business associate agreement scoped to the voice channel by name; and pilot against real call volume, including a full on-call weekend, before signing. An orthopedic phone line needs logic a generic voice agent doesn't ship with: subspecialty and body-part routing, post-op call volume treated as a clinical triage signal rather than just workload, protection of same-day surgical windows, enforcement of referral/imaging prerequisites, and handling for workers' comp and employer-referral intake. Why the phone goes unanswered: the same MGMA staffing math that makes medical assistants the hardest role to recruit hits orthopedic front desks directly, and the volume is heavier than most realize, 8.6 calls per on-call shift with over half about pain, prescriptions, and wounds (Tideman et al., 2023), only 4.1% resulting in an ED visit. Timing compounds it: 28.5% of calls arrive outside business hours (NextPhone, 2026) against Clinekt's own 82% after-hours booking-attempt figure. Proof: a multi-provider orthopedic group using Clinekt's Inbound and Recall agents turned 263 qualified surgical leads into 159 booked appointments in a single quarter, a 60% booking rate, without adding front-desk headcount.

FAQ digest: An AI voice agent for an orthopedic practice answers the phone, screens the request against orthopedic-specific logic (body part, surgical status, urgency), and books, reschedules, or cancels directly in the schedule rather than only relaying a message. Voice is one channel inside a broader AI receptionist deployment; a separate guide covers the channel-agnostic picture. A well-built agent is trained on red-flag language and escalates immediately rather than trying to resolve urgent symptoms itself. Most calls into an orthopedic practice are administrative or routine follow-up, not acute clinical conversations, which is why patients generally accept a fast, well-identified AI handoff. A voice agent does not replace on-call staff; it absorbs high-volume, repeatable call load so on-call staff can focus on calls that need clinical judgment.

# AI Answering Service for an Orthopedic Practice: What It Should Actually Do
Source: https://clinekthealth.com/blog/ai-answering-service-for-orthopedic-practice
Published: 2026-08-28

Direct answer: An AI answering service for an orthopedic practice should triage every after-hours call into three lanes: a true surgical emergency routed to the on-call surgeon immediately, a routine post-op question answered or booked without a callback, and a workers' comp or attorney call captured correctly so it does not stall a claim. A message-only service that just logs a callback for the morning solves half the problem.

Key takeaways: An orthopedic AI answering service should triage every call into three lanes (true emergencies escalated immediately, routine post-op questions resolved or booked, workers' comp/attorney calls captured with the right claim details). A 2026 study of 45,216 total hip and knee arthroplasty patients found perioperative call-and-message touchpoints rose 105% for TKA and 121% for THA over the study period, with each patient averaging 4.4 postoperative calls in the first 90 days (Lam et al., Journal of Bone and Joint Surgery, May 2026). Nearly a third of orthopedic trauma patients call the practice within 14 days of discharge, most often about pain control, wound or dressing questions, and discharge medications (Hadeed et al., Journal of Orthopaedic Trauma, March 2017). Across Clinekt deployments, 82% of patients try to book outside office hours. The AI-answering-service category for orthopedic practices is still open: general-medicine vendors dominate, few differentiate triage logic for a surgical on-call line.

Section summaries: The after-hours line is a different job than the daytime front desk because the call mix shifts toward patients who just had surgery rather than new-patient scheduling and referral intake; the Lam et al. (2026) and Hadeed et al. (2017) studies quantify that shift. What an orthopedic AI answering service should triage for specifically: surgical site concerns (redness, drainage, fever, opened wound), pain out of proportion to the timeline, DVT/PE warning signs (the single highest-stakes triage decision), workers' comp and attorney calls (claim number, adjuster, employer, date of injury), and medication/routine "is this normal" questions (the highest-volume, easiest-to-resolve category). A five-question evaluation checklist: how does it tell an emergency from a routine call, what happens the moment it identifies one, can it capture a workers' comp call correctly, does it cover every after-hours gap (nights/weekends/holidays/lunch), and can staff audit every call including the ones deemed not urgent. Differentiated from the AI front desk (daytime, end-to-end resolution), the AI receptionist guide (channel-agnostic evaluation), and the AI voice agent checklist (voice-channel specific) already published for orthopedic practices; parallels the existing dental-ai-answering-service post with an orthopedic-specific emergency profile. Proof: a multi-provider orthopedic group using Clinekt's Inbound agent turned 263 qualified surgical leads into 159 booked appointments in a single quarter, a 60% booking rate.

FAQ digest: An AI answering service for an orthopedic practice answers calls the practice cannot cover live (nights, weekends, holidays), triages true emergencies from routine post-op questions, and either resolves the call or escalates to the on-call surgeon. It is only safe for a real emergency if its triage logic is reliable and reviewable; ask any vendor to walk through the actual logic and review real transcripts. A human on-call surgeon is still required; AI replaces the message-taking and triage layer, not the physician's clinical decision. It differs from an AI front desk, which resolves daytime scheduling and referral calls end to end, versus after-hours/overflow coverage specifically. Workers' comp calls after hours should be captured with claim number, adjuster contact, employer, and date of injury on the first call.

# Orthopedic Patient Intake Software: What to Look for Before You Buy
Source: https://clinekthealth.com/blog/orthopedic-patient-intake-software
Published: 2026-08-31

Direct answer: Orthopedic patient intake software should capture a complete, subspecialty-correct picture before the visit ever happens: the injury or complaint in the patient's own words, a referring physician and any imaging already on file, insurance and workers' comp details, and consent specific to a surgical consult, not a generic new-patient packet copied from primary care. A form that only digitizes a paper clipboard still leaves staff to sort out which surgeon the patient actually needs, whether a referral or imaging order exists, and whether the visit even qualifies for the insurance on file.

Key takeaways: Orthopedic patient intake software needs to capture injury mechanism, referring physician and imaging status, workers' comp details, and subspecialty routing, none of which a generic new-patient form is built to ask for. Sending a pre-visit reminder through a patient portal or email nearly doubled pre-visit form completion compared to no reminder at all, 49% versus 30%, in a randomized controlled trial of orthopedic ambulatory patients (Yedulla et al., Journal of Bone and Joint Surgery, 2023). More than half of total joint replacement patients need prior authorization before surgery can even be scheduled, and the average approval takes over three weeks (Abe et al., Journal of Arthroplasty, 2024). Across Clinekt deployments, 82% of patients try to book or complete intake outside normal office hours. Orthopedic patient intake automation is still a fragmented category: most vendors sell general medical intake with an orthopedic label on it, not intake logic built around subspecialty routing, imaging status, and workers' comp from the start.

Section summaries: Orthopedic intake needs to go beyond digitizing the clipboard by capturing mechanism of injury, referring physician and imaging status, and workers' comp details so the visit is already routed correctly by the time the patient arrives. Subspecialty routing, prior authorization, and workers' comp documentation are three things a general medical intake form was never built to ask about. A 2024 study of primary total joint arthroplasty patients found 56.4% of total hip replacement patients and 54% of total knee replacement patients required prior authorization before surgery could be scheduled, with average approval taking 26.3 days for hip and 33.7 days for knee (Abe et al., Journal of Arthroplasty, 2024). A double-blinded, prospective randomized controlled trial of orthopedic ambulatory patients found a pre-visit reminder sent through a patient portal or email nearly doubled completion of pre-visit forms versus no reminder: 49% versus 30% (Yedulla et al., Journal of Bone and Joint Surgery, 2023). Five things a generic form misses: mechanism of injury, referring physician and existing imaging, workers' comp claim details, insurance verification and prior-authorization status, and subspecialty-specific consent and pre-visit instructions. A five-check evaluation checklist: test subspecialty routing on a real intake, ask how workers' comp and injury-mechanism fields are captured, confirm insurance and prior-authorization status is flagged before the visit, check EHR write-back instead of a PDF export, and ask for a completion-rate number from an orthopedic customer. Differentiated from orthopedic patient engagement software (full perioperative timeline) and orthopedic referral management software (what happens after a referral arrives) by scoping specifically to the intake step itself. Proof: Baldwin Bone and Joint, a multi-provider orthopedic group, generated 263 qualified surgical leads and booked 159 appointments in a single quarter, a 60% booking rate, using Clinekt's Inbound agent on the calls, referrals, and intake the practice was already receiving.

FAQ digest: Orthopedic patient intake software collects a new or returning patient's history, injury details, insurance, and consent before the visit, with orthopedic-specific fields for mechanism of injury, referring physician and imaging, workers' comp claim details, and subspecialty routing that a general medical intake form does not ask for. It differs from general medical intake software because it also needs to capture mechanism of injury, route by subspecialty, flag prior-authorization needs early, and handle workers' comp documentation. It does not replace front-desk staff; it replaces the repetitive parts of data collection and routing while clinical judgment and phone conversations still go to a person. It can shorten prior-authorization delays by flagging a likely need and starting documentation at intake, though the approval itself still runs through the payer, commonly three to five weeks for total joint procedures. It indirectly reduces no-shows since completing intake before the visit is one of the strongest predictors that a patient shows up prepared, and the right pre-visit reminder channel measurably increases completion.

# Orthopedic Patient Activation Software: What the Results Actually Look Like
Source: https://clinekthealth.com/blog/orthopedic-patient-activation-results
Published: 2026-09-01

Direct answer: The way to judge AI patient activation software is by booked appointments over a stated time period, not a vendor's slide deck, and the practices actually running it already have real numbers to show. Most vendor pages lead with adjectives instead of a number that says what happened, to whom, and over what window.

Key takeaways: An MGMA Stat poll of practice leaders in May 2026 found only 46% said AI tools actually made providers more productive; 27% saw no gains at all and 14% were not sure. 82% of patients try to book an appointment outside normal office hours, the baseline volume any activation number has to be measured against. One multi-provider orthopedic group running Clinekt's Inbound agent produced 263 qualified surgical leads and 159 booked appointments in a single quarter, a 60% booking rate, calculated the same way any practice could calculate its own. A case study is marketing copy until it names the practice type, the time window, and the exact formula behind the number. The right question to ask a vendor is never "does it work," it is "what does work mean here, measured how, over what period."

Section summaries: A real result names four things: the practice type, the time window, the raw counts behind the percentage, and how the percentage was calculated; a promise with no practice named, no time window, and no denominator is not a result. An MGMA Stat poll of 257 practice leaders (May 12, 2026) found 46% said AI made providers more productive, 27% saw no gains, 14% were unsure, and 13% were not using AI yet, evidence that vendor productivity claims and measured results are frequently two different things. Baldwin Bone and Joint, a multi-provider orthopedic group, produced 263 qualified surgical leads and 159 booked appointments in a single quarter using Clinekt's Inbound agent, a checkable 60% booking rate from work the practice was already doing. Booking rate should be booked appointments divided by qualified leads over a stated period; ways the calculation gets inflated include counting every form submission as a lead, counting an appointment as booked before it survives to being confirmed, and reporting a percentage with no denominator. Five questions to ask a vendor before trusting its numbers: what practice type and size produced this number, over what exact time window, what are the raw counts behind the percentage, is this total volume or only the volume the software touched, and can you talk to the practice directly. A real activation number is not an ROI guarantee; it promises a checkable booking rate, not a dollar figure or a specific revenue timeline.

FAQ digest: Patient activation software turns inbound patient demand, calls, web inquiries, referrals, and follow-up outreach into completed, booked appointments, rather than answering the phone or sending a reminder in isolation. There is no single publicly benchmarked industry standard yet for a good orthopedic booking rate; a defensible number states the raw counts and time window behind it, not a bare percentage. Vendor case studies vary widely because "qualified lead" and "booked appointment" are not standardized definitions, and an unstated denominator can describe almost any underlying volume. A good result from one orthopedic practice does not guarantee the same result elsewhere since practice size, referral mix, payer mix, and existing front desk process all affect the outcome. Before trusting a vendor's numbers, ask for the practice type, the exact time window, the raw lead and appointment counts, and a reference practice willing to confirm the number directly.

# Orthopedic Patient Check-In Software: What to Look for Before You Buy
Source: https://clinekthealth.com/blog/orthopedic-patient-check-in-software
Published: 2026-09-02

Direct answer: Orthopedic patient check-in software confirms insurance, collects any updated paperwork, and tells your front desk the moment a patient has arrived, all before that patient sits down in the waiting room. Most orthopedic practices still run this step through a person standing at a front desk with a clipboard, and digitizing check-in only helps if it actually removes work from that desk instead of adding a second system for staff to watch.

Key takeaways: 83% of practices still check patients in primarily at the front desk, with only 7% online, 3% by phone, 3% by text, and 3% by kiosk, per a 2022 MGMA Stat poll of 652 medical groups. Among practices that do send patients a digital registration link, only about half actually complete it that way, per the same MGMA data. No-shows, online scheduling, phone access, and wait times ranked as the top four patient access priorities for 2026 in an MGMA Stat poll of 236 medical groups fielded December 2025, and check-in sits directly upstream of all four. A 2018 Vitals study found 30% of patients have left a physician's office before being seen because of a long wait. Orthopedic check-in has its own failure points a generic medical check-in tool does not handle well: verifying which subspecialty a patient is there for, confirming imaging or a referral already exists, and flagging a workers' comp visit before the visit starts.

Section summaries: At minimum, orthopedic check-in software replaces the paper clipboard and sign-in sheet, letting a patient confirm arrival, update address and insurance, and sign outstanding forms digitally. The harder job is making that confirmation trigger something useful: real-time staff notification, a copay or balance flagged before the visit, and anything unusual (a workers' comp claim, an insurance mismatch, an incomplete form) surfaced automatically. Five things orthopedic check-in should include: real-time arrival alerts, insurance and copay verification at arrival, subspecialty and referral confirmation, workers' comp flagging, and a fast in-person fallback for the roughly half of patients who never open a digital registration link. A five-check evaluation checklist: test it on a real multi-subspecialty scenario, confirm real-time staff notification, ask what happens when a patient never opens the digital link, check EHR and practice management write-back, and ask for a completion-rate number instead of a features list. Differentiated from orthopedic patient intake software (what gets collected before the visit) and orthopedic AI scheduling software (the booking itself); check-in is the last checkpoint before a booked appointment becomes a completed one. Proof: Baldwin Bone and Joint, a multi-provider orthopedic group, generated 263 qualified surgical leads and booked 159 appointments in a single quarter, a 60% booking rate, using Clinekt's Inbound agent on the calls, referrals, and intake the practice was already receiving; a booking that stalls at check-in on a missed insurance flag or an uncaught workers' comp claim is a booking that has to be redone.

FAQ digest: Orthopedic patient check-in software confirms a patient has arrived, verifies insurance and updates demographics, and alerts staff in real time, with orthopedic-specific checks for subspecialty routing and workers' comp status that a general medical check-in tool does not run. It differs from patient intake because intake collects information before the visit while check-in confirms that information is still accurate and starts the visit itself. It does not replace front-desk staff; it removes the repetitive parts (confirming arrival, verifying insurance, updating a form) so staff spend time on patients who need a real conversation. About half of patients complete digital check-in when offered a link, per MGMA data, which is why an in-person fallback still matters. It indirectly reduces no-shows and cancellations since a slow, frustrating check-in experience once makes a patient more likely to cancel or no-show the next visit.

# CRM Software for Orthopedic Clinics: What to Look for Before You Buy
Source: https://clinekthealth.com/blog/crm-software-for-orthopedic-clinics
Published: 2026-09-03

Direct answer: CRM software for an orthopedic clinic should track every referral, lead, and patient relationship in one record, but tracking a relationship and acting on it are two different jobs, and most CRM software only does the first one. A CRM logs who called and when someone last followed up; it does not answer the phone, work a referral the day it arrives, or carry a dormant patient back to a booked visit.

Key takeaways: CRM software for orthopedic clinics should centralize referral source, subspecialty, treatment status, and next-follow-up date in one patient record. Most CRM tools log and organize contacts; very few call, text, or schedule on their own. Definitive Healthcare's HospitalView data (May 2026) shows the CRM tools ranked highest by total installations, Epic's Cheers (428 installations, 23.6%), Salesforce Essentials (364, 20.1%), and Microsoft Dynamics 365 (276, 15.2%), are built and bought for hospital systems, not small orthopedic groups. A May 2025 MGMA Stat poll of 420 practice leaders found 47% name medical assistants the hardest role to recruit, the same front-office roles usually responsible for working a CRM's queue by hand. A CRM paired with software that acts on the record it holds recovers leads a CRM alone only tracks.

Section summaries: CRM stands for customer relationship management; in orthopedics it means one record holding referral source, subspecialty, injury type, insurance and prior-authorization status, treatment plan stage, and dormant/reactivation status, not just a name and phone number. A CRM is a system of record, not a system of action: it stores that a referral came in or a follow-up was missed, but someone still has to notice the entry and act, often after the window that mattered has closed. Mainstream CRM leaderboards are written for hospital systems (Epic Cheers, Salesforce, Microsoft Dynamics), so an independent orthopedic group evaluating CRM software against that leaderboard is comparing itself to the wrong buyer. A six-item evaluation checklist: map actual lead sources first, ask whether the CRM acts or only logs, test referral capture specifically, check how dormant patients get flagged and worked, confirm EHR/PM write-back, and ask for a follow-up-rate number instead of a record count. Clinekt does not replace a practice's CRM, EHR, or practice management system; Inbound, Recall, and Outbound act on the same record those systems already hold, answering after-hours referrals, working the dormant list, and reaching net-new demand, instead of only logging the touchpoint. Proof: Baldwin Bone and Joint, a multi-provider orthopedic group, generated 263 qualified surgical leads and booked 159 appointments in a single quarter, a 60% booking rate, using Clinekt's system to act on the referrals, calls, and dormant patients a CRM alone would only track.

FAQ digest: CRM software for orthopedic clinics centralizes every patient and referral contact in one record, tracking referral source, subspecialty, treatment stage, and follow-up status. A CRM is not the same as an EHR (clinical documentation) or a practice management system (scheduling and billing); it is built to track relationships and leads, including people who are not yet patients. Clinekt does not replace a practice's CRM; it works on top of the CRM, EHR, or PM system a practice already runs. A good orthopedic CRM should track, at minimum, referring physician and practice, injury or subspecialty, insurance and prior-authorization status, and treatment plan stage. Inbound call handling and referral response typically start working from go-live; dormant-patient reactivation takes a bit longer since it depends on the size and age of the current dormant list.

# Orthopedic Patient Recall Software: What to Look for Before You Buy
Source: https://clinekthealth.com/blog/orthopedic-patient-recall-software
Published: 2026-09-04

Direct answer: Orthopedic patient recall software should catch every post-op check, surveillance-imaging visit, and injection-cycle patient who is due for care and has nothing booked, and most recall software on the market is built for a dental hygiene interval that orthopedic practices don't run. A six-month cleaning cadence is predictable and identical for every patient; an orthopedic due list mixes a two-week wound check, a six-week fracture follow-up, a one-year implant surveillance x-ray, and a repeat cortisone injection on different clocks.

Key takeaways: Orthopedic recall doesn't run on a fixed interval; post-op check windows, implant-surveillance imaging, and injection-cycle timing all vary by procedure. A Journal of Bone and Joint Surgery study of 776 total joint arthroplasty patients (Clohisy et al., 2008) found clinical follow-up compliance fell to 61% at one year and 36% at two years when recall relied on nothing but a verbal request from the surgeon. A 2024 JAAOS Global Research & Reviews study of 518 orthopaedic trauma surgery patients (Bender et al.) found 15% missed at least one of their first two scheduled post-op follow-up visits. Good orthopedic recall software segments the due list by procedure and post-op window, not a single "time since last visit" clock, and books the visit directly when a patient responds instead of generating a callback task.

Section summaries: Orthopedic recall software needs a layer generic recall tools don't have: the due list itself has to be built around procedure type and post-op timeline, not one fixed interval. A single practice carries post-op wound checks at 2 weeks, fracture follow-ups at 6 weeks, therapy-progress checks at 3 months, implant-surveillance imaging at 1/2/5/10 years, and injection-cycle patients due again in 3-6 months, all at once. An orthopedic recall list actually contains five patient types: post-op check patients (segmented by procedure), implant-surveillance patients (on implant-specific schedules), injection-cycle patients, consult-pending surgical patients, and therapy-referral patients due for a check-in. Six things orthopedic recall software should do: segment the due list by procedure and post-op window, flag surveillance-imaging patients on implant-specific schedules, contact patients on more than one channel, follow up more than once, book the visit directly against open scheduling, and report recall completion by patient type rather than one blended number. Missed post-op follow-up carries clinical stakes beyond scheduling: it's the visit where a surgeon checks a wound for infection, confirms a fracture is healing on track, or catches a complication early enough to manage in the office instead of the emergency department. Recall differs from reactivation: recall reaches active patients due for a known next step, reactivation reaches patients who have gone fully dormant (12+ months). Proof: Baldwin Bone and Joint, a multi-provider orthopedic group, generated 263 qualified surgical leads and booked 159 appointments in a single quarter, a 60% booking rate, running Clinekt's patient activation agents, of which the Recall Agent works the orthopedic due list on a standing cadence segmented by procedure and post-op window.

FAQ digest: Orthopedic patient recall software identifies patients due for a post-op check, implant-surveillance x-ray, or repeat injection, contacts them automatically, and books the appointment. Recall differs from reactivation in that recall reaches active patients not yet dormant, while reactivation reaches patients gone 12+ months without a visit. Hygiene-style recall software fails in orthopedics because it assumes one fixed interval, while orthopedic due lists mix post-op windows, implant-surveillance schedules, and injection cycles on their own timelines. Recall-list patients include post-op check patients, implant-surveillance imaging patients, injection-cycle patients, consult-pending surgical patients, and therapy-referral patients. Clinekt does not replace an EHR's recall report; it works the due list the EHR already generates and acts on it: contacting patients, following up more than once, and booking the visit directly.

# Orthopedic Patient No-Show Rates: What Drives Them and How to Cut Them
Source: https://clinekthealth.com/blog/orthopedic-patient-no-show-rates
Published: 2026-09-07

Direct answer: Orthopedic no-show rates run from about 7% at established private practices to 11% to 25% at academic and referral-based orthopedic clinics, and two new 2025-2026 studies agree on what predicts a miss: a patient's prior no-show history and whether their appointment was confirmed. Confirmation cuts the odds of a no-show by roughly 75% to 80% in both studies.

Key takeaways: A 2026 study of 17,614 total joint arthroplasty patients at a single academic center found a 6.86% no-show rate, but patients with a heavy prior no-show history were nearly ten times more likely to miss again (Rehman et al., Arthroplasty Today, 2026). A 2025 study of 11,667 orthopedic oncology appointments found an 11% no-show rate, with appointment confirmation cutting the odds of a miss by about 81% (Journal of the American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons, August 2025). Both studies agree prior attendance behavior and confirmation status predict a miss far better than demographics. Machine-learning risk models in both studies could flag the highest-risk 20% of appointments and catch roughly 60% of eventual no-shows. Across Clinekt deployments, 82% of patients try to book outside office hours.

Section summaries: No-show rates vary sharply by setting: 6.86% at a joint-replacement academic clinic, 11% at an orthopedic oncology clinic, versus the MGMA single-specialty median of 6.81% for established private practices. An August 2025 MGMA Stat poll of 265 medical groups found 73% reported no-shows stayed the same or decreased year over year, while 27% said they increased. Both studies found the same two predictors: prior no-show history (adjusted odds ratio up to 9.86 for the heaviest-history patients) and appointment confirmation (adjusted odds ratio 0.24 and 0.193, meaning confirmation cuts the odds of a miss by 75-80%). Six steps to reduce orthopedic no-shows: confirm every appointment, flag repeat no-show history and treat it differently, shorten lead time on new-patient and referral consults, enable confirmation and rescheduling at any hour, route post-op and recall patients through a standing follow-up list, and measure your rate against the right benchmark. Generic reminder blasts fall short in a surgical specialty because a missed new-patient consult after a referral can be a lost surgical case, and a missed post-op follow-up is a compliance and outcomes risk, not just an empty slot. Proof: Baldwin Bone and Joint, a multi-provider orthopedic group, generated 263 qualified surgical leads and booked 159 appointments in a single quarter, a 60% booking rate, largely from demand the practice was already receiving but not fully converting.

# Orthopedic Patient Communications Software: What to Look for Before You Buy
Source: https://clinekthealth.com/blog/orthopedic-patient-communications-software
Published: 2026-09-08

Direct answer: Orthopedic patient communications software is the messaging layer that sends and receives appointment reminders, referral and imaging updates, pre-op and post-op instructions, billing notices, and recall outreach across phone, text, email, and portal, in both directions, from one connected record. Patients rank phone calls and text messages well above portals and email for these updates, so the software's real job is to meet patients on the channels they actually use.

Key takeaways: A 2025 study of 472 total joint arthroplasty patients found phone calls the most preferred communication method (53.5% ranked them first), followed by text messages (35.4%); patient portals ranked last, with 55.8% naming a portal their least preferred channel (Arthroplasty Today, 2025). 93% of patients responded positively to one-way updates and 92.5% wanted two-way access such as telehealth or direct messaging. A UK orthopedic fracture clinic found smartphone ownership rose from 66.3% to 84.5% between 2019 and 2024, and email preference rose from 68.9% to 80.6% over the same period (Cureus, 2024). An October 2024 MGMA Stat poll of 302 medical groups found practices investing nearly six times more in AI for clinical documentation (59%) than for patient communication (10%). Across Clinekt deployments, 82% of patients try to book outside office hours.

Section summaries: An orthopedic practice sends at least six distinct message types across a patient's episode of care (appointment reminders, referral and imaging status, pre-op instructions, post-op check-ins and recall, billing, and outcome surveys), and most practices run each through a different disconnected tool. The clearest preference data comes from a 2025 study of 472 joint arthroplasty patients: phone calls won decisively (53.5% most preferred, 12.8% least), text messages came second (35.4% most preferred, 5.3% least), email third (26.7%/17.4%), and portals finished last (9.4% most preferred, 55.8% least preferred); 95.6% of patients were willing to give their surgeon's team a cell phone number and email address. A UK longitudinal study (99 patients in 2019, 103 in 2024) found the shift toward digital channels accelerating on its own, with smartphone ownership and email preference both rising over five years. Investment lags patient preference: an MGMA poll of 302 medical groups found only 10% of AI investment priority went to patient communication versus 59% to documentation. Six checks before buying: match the channel mix to patient preference (phone and text first), confirm every channel is two-way, cover all six message types in one record, verify consent and carrier compliance are automatic, confirm write-back to the chart, and test what happens when a question needs a real answer. Clinekt's Inbound Agent answers every conversation on the phone or by text day or night, and the Recall Agent keeps a conversation open until it resolves instead of sending one message and moving on. Proof: Baldwin Bone and Joint, a multi-provider orthopedic group, generated 263 qualified surgical leads and booked 159 appointments in a single quarter, a 60% booking rate, largely by keeping conversations open with patients other systems let go quiet.

FAQ digest: Orthopedic patients prefer phone calls and text messages by a wide margin over patient portals and email for practice communication (53.5% and 35.4% versus 9.4% most-preferred, respectively). A portal-only strategy misses most of what patients want, since 92.5% also want two-way channels like telehealth or direct messaging. 95.6% of patients are willing to give their care team a cell phone number and email address. Patient preference is trending toward more digital channels over time, not fewer, as smartphone ownership climbs. Patient communications software differs from a patient portal by covering phone, text, email, and portal together from one record, rather than relying on the single channel patients rank last.

FAQ digest: A normal orthopedic no-show rate depends on setting: 6.81% MGMA median for established private practices, 6.86% to 11% for academic/referral-based orthopedic clinics. The single strongest predictor is a patient's own prior no-show history, with confirmation status the strongest predictor a practice can actively influence. Reminders alone don't fully fix orthopedic no-shows since confirmation and attendance history predict a miss more strongly than whether a reminder was sent. Scheduling teams can predict which appointments are highest risk (AUC 0.80-0.83 in two 2025-2026 studies, catching about 60% of no-shows when flagging the riskiest 20%), but that supplements confirming every appointment rather than replacing it. Confirming appointments addresses the cause of a no-show; a fee only addresses the aftermath and recovers a fraction of the lost visit.
